transcript.text: If you had to guess, what menu sells
more? Menu number one or menu number
two? Researchers actually looked at this
and figured out what the answer was. So,
they did this test with a bunch of jam
stands where they had one stand that had
24 types of jam and another stand that
had only six. And they had people walk
up to it. And what was interesting is
that one of these jam stands converted
significantly higher than the other. And
you might think, "Oh, the more selection
people have, the more likely they are to
buy the perfect thing for them." But in
reality, what ended up happening is that
people were 10 times more likely to buy
when they had fewer selections because
the decision was easier. We actually
implemented this kind of perspective
with a portfolio company right as we
invested. And they had a kind of like
choose your own adventure type thing.
Like, "Whatever you can think of, we'll
sell it to you." And so, what we looked
at when we pulled all the data was we
figured out that there are actually two
customer avatars they had and they
bought two very different sets of
things. And so, we said, "Okay, what is
80% of the time this person buy and what
is 80% of the time this person buy?" And
then we completely consolidated to
choice A and choice B for customer A and
customer B. What happened is we were
able to actually sell more people at
higher prices, templatize the solution
on the back end so we were able to
expand margin because we were able to do
the same thing for more times for more
people and able to on-ramp salespeople
faster cuz they didn't have to learn the
whole menu, they only had to learn two
things. And then customers transacted
faster and we cut the sales time in
half. If you believe in free markets is
